BOOTH LIGHTBUILD 130FOR THE LISTENING ROOM

BOOTH LIGHT

Record, cut and take notes on a podcast interview. Edit the audio and place your episode in the Listening Room Archive.Every storyteller decides who listens, for how long, and when to erase their story.
▶The Listening RoomListen on Spotify · opens in a new tab

Two ways to use Booth Light. Same app, same features.

On a laptop, as a file

Most private. Get the file from your instructor (AirDrop, USB or the class QR code) and open it in Chrome or Firefox. Nothing about you reaches any company. The file does not update itself: get the new file from your instructor when a new version comes out.

On a phone or laptop, at the web address

academicfreedom.github.io/booth-light. Nothing to download; add it to your Home Screen if you like. It updates itself. GitHub (owned by Microsoft) logs each visit’s IP address and time; it never receives your recordings.

Either way, your recordings stay on the device you recorded on. Export them to move them.

Download the laptop file

  1. Open the address in Safari while connected.
  2. Tap Share (the square with an arrow), then Add to Home Screen, then Add.
  3. Open Booth Light from its Home Screen icon and allow the microphone. Do this before you record: Safari deletes the stored work of websites not opened for 7 days; Home Screen apps are exempt.
  4. Recording stops if the screen locks or you switch apps. Keep the screen on.

Once Booth Light is on your Home Screen, open it in aeroplane mode (Wi-Fi and mobile data off). The phone then makes no network connection, so neither your network nor GitHub receives anything. If you open it while connected, the phone checks GitHub for an update, and that check is logged like your first visit. Your recordings, notes and texts are not part of that check: Booth Light never sends them. A file you export stays on the phone if you save it to On My iPhone. Saved to iCloud Drive, it is copied to Apple’s servers. If Safari is on under Settings › your name › iCloud, Apple receives the address of this page in your Safari history, not your recordings.

  1. Open the address in Chrome while connected.
  2. Tap ⋮ (top right), then Add to Home screen (on some phones: Install app), then Install.
  3. Open Booth Light from its Home Screen icon and allow the microphone.
  4. Recording stops if the screen locks or you switch apps. Keep the screen on.

Once Booth Light is on your Home Screen, turn on Airplane mode and open it. The phone then makes no network connection, so neither your network nor GitHub receives anything. If you open it while connected, Chrome checks GitHub for an update, and that check is logged like your first visit. Your recordings, notes and texts are not part of that check: Booth Light never sends them. Exports are saved to the Download folder on your phone. They stay on the phone unless you move them to Google Drive or share them. If Chrome sync is on, Google receives the address of this page in your browsing history, not your recordings.

  1. Opening the page while connected: the phone asks the network for the address of the site (a DNS lookup) and starts an encrypted connection whose first message names the site in plain text (TLS SNI). The network (WWU Wi-Fi or your phone carrier) can log your device, your login on eduroam, the site name, the time and how much data moved.
  2. The network cannot read the page or anything you type or record: the connection is encrypted (https), and Booth Light sends none of it.
  3. GitHub logs your internet address, the time, the files requested and your phone and browser type. It receives no recordings.
  4. After you add it to the Home Screen, the phone keeps a copy (a service worker). Opened with no connection, it contacts nothing. Opened while connected, it asks GitHub for the newest page each time it opens; each time is logged like the first visit.
  5. How long WWU and GitHub keep these logs, and who may obtain them, is set by WWU policy, Washington State law and GitHub’s terms. Booth Light cannot change that.
  6. The laptop file is not loaded from the internet, so none of this happens when it opens. It connects to GitHub only for the withdrawn list and the Earlier seasons shelf.

        5Who can hear this recording?

        In a time of increased surveillance, any copy of an interview that an institution or third party company holds can be requested by third parties, leaked, or sold. This app mitigates for that risk by keeping the recording on your device and by authorizing all contributors to decide who may access their stories at any time.

        Episode producers and storytellers can select who may hear their podcast episodes in The Process Consent options below. Each person on the recording chooses the option that best suits their own risk assessment. The recording is shared only as widely as the most private choice. You can choose a codename, not a real name, if and when necessary.

        Sovereign tech

        1. Recordings and notes are stored in this browser’s storage (IndexedDB) on this device. There is no account and no server, so no company holds a copy.
        2. Once open, the page makes two kinds of network request, both to GitHub: the withdrawn list, if your device holds a class episode, and the Earlier seasons shelf, when you unlock it or play from it. The page sends your recordings, notes and texts nowhere by itself.
        3. A file leaves the device only when you press Export. It is saved to the folder you choose.

        Process consent

        1. Five listening levels, from the most private to the widest: 1 Nowhere else (only the episode producer hears it, on the device they recorded with); 2 On the podcast producer’s computer; 3 In the classroom, during listening sessions; 4 At the Listening Party, with guests the class curates. The episode plays at the most private level anyone on it chose. Level 5 is a future feature and cannot be chosen.
        2. Each person gets an erase code. Today the code works only in the class archive on the podcast producer’s computer. A storyteller who wants to withdraw tells the episode producer or the podcast producer, and the withdrawal is applied within 72 hours. A future version will let a storyteller erase their recording from their own phone.
        3. Every record the app writes uses the codenames you type, not real names.

        Tap a person, then a level on the left.

        The apps

        Sovereign or transparent · each handed over as a folder, by USB or AirDrop

        Booth Lightsovereign

        Records, cuts and annotates interviews on the student’s own device, with no account and no copy on any server; each storyteller decides who listens, for how long, and holds a code that erases the episode. Opened as a file it connects to GitHub only for the withdrawn list and the Earlier seasons shelf; the phone copy loads from GitHub, which logs the phone’s IP address and the time.

        Safelightsovereign

        Prepares files for a border crossing or a device search: seals them to a key that stays behind, renames them so their names reveal nothing, and proves nothing changed. It saves nothing about your files in the browser and makes no internet connection; your exports, browser history and the Mac’s recent-files records remain.

        Brightlightsovereign

        Reads what a file says about itself (where an email travelled, what made a document, what it said before an edit) with open-source tools anyone can re-run for the same answer. It saves nothing about your files in the browser and connects only to your own Mac (127.0.0.1); exports, history and recent-files records remain.

        Firstlightsovereign

        Gives footage a SHA-256 fingerprint the moment it lands, so anyone can check later that a clip was not altered. Runs in the browser on your own computer with no internet connection.

        Skylighttransparent

        Collects stills and clips from public, open-licence cameras around the world for filmmaking. It connects to those camera servers on purpose, so they see your IP address and the time; nothing of yours is sent, and frames save to the folder you choose.

        Limelightsovereign

        Projection mapping for screenings, actions and teach-ins, run from your own laptop with no account and no internet connection; projects and media stay on that laptop.

        Ghostlightsovereign

        Projection for actions, run from a USB stick on any computer with no network connection; what it shows stays on the stick and in that browser tab.

        Risk & safety

        2025–2026, with sources

        55,318

        Devices searched by US Customs and Border Protection in fiscal year 2025, up 17.6% in one year. 13,590 of them belonged to US citizens. Since 1 January 2026 the search rules also name flash drives, SIM cards and smart watches.

        CBP figures, reported by CBC News, 8 March 2026

        100,000+

        Visas revoked in 2025, about 8,000 of them student visas. Since June 2025 every student-visa applicant must set their social media to public for review; officers are told to look for “hostility” toward the United States.

        US State Department, 12 January 2026; AP, 19 June 2025

        1 in 4

        WWU faculty who said they had been targeted for their work, of 202 who answered a 2025 Faculty Senate survey: most often for work on immigration, LGBTQ issues, climate change and Israel–Palestine, mostly by email and on social media. Four of them named public-records requests as the method.

        WWU Faculty Senate survey, osf.io/preprints/osf/amr9j_v1; reported by the Brechner Center, 1 May 2025

        100+

        Open-records requests filed at 19 public universities against at least 30 climate researchers in five years, more than half of them since November 2024. They demand emails, drafts and correspondence.

        POLITICO investigation, 25 September 2026; Nature, October 2026

        Dozens

        Faculty and staff punished over social-media posts in the weeks after Charlie Kirk was killed in September 2025. Clemson fired three. Student groups screenshotted the posts and sent them to lawmakers and donors.

        AAUP count via Times Higher Education, 25 September 2025; The Post and Courier, 6 May 2026

        $1.5 million

        What Rutgers spent on a Motorola Avigilon AI camera system that reads plates, recognises faces and tracks people across campus; it tested facial recognition without telling students or faculty. Emory took down its Flock plate readers in September 2026 after protests; one search had been logged under the reason “Protest”.

        NJ.com, 13 October 2026; The Emory Wheel, 2026

        $17 million

        Cal State’s contract with OpenAI for ChatGPT Edu; the University of California plans system-wide contracts with Anthropic and OpenAI. Every prompt goes to the company’s servers. “Not used for training” is a clause in a contract, not a property of the tool.

        CalMatters, 1 May 2026; Daily Bruin, 2 October 2026

        14%

        Faculty nationwide who were disciplined or threatened with discipline for their teaching, research, talks or speech off campus, in a 2024 survey of 6,269 faculty at 55 US four-year colleges. 35% said they had recently toned down their writing for fear of controversy; 23% worry about losing their jobs over something misunderstood.

        FIRE, Silence in the Classroom: The 2024 FIRE Faculty Survey Report

        How the harm happens, in five steps

        1. Collect Phones, accounts, campus cameras and class apps record what people do, say and write.
        2. Concentrate One company or one university server keeps everyone’s records together.
        3. List Those records make a person findable: a student on a visa, a protester, a faculty member who filed a complaint.
        4. Hand over The records go to someone else: through a subpoena, a public-records request, a data breach or a sale.
        5. Act Someone uses them: a phone search at the border, a revoked visa, a firing, an investigation.

        Every number above is one of these steps. A class app that keeps students’ work on a company’s server is step 2.

        Feminist red-teaming

        Red-teaming is a security practice: you attack your own system before an adversary does, then fix what broke. AI companies pay red teams to make their AI models (statistical models trained on huge amounts of text) produce harm before release. Feminist red-teaming takes the practice into the classroom and changes four things.

        Who is on the red team

        Not a security firm. The people with the least institutional power: storytellers, international and undocumented students, trans students, students whose families are organising. They test each feature against their own exposure, and the most cautious of them sets the limit for everyone.

        Who counts as the attacker

        In a university the attacker is rarely a hacker first. It is the institution that keeps the files and answers subpoenas and records requests; the vendor that keeps the copies and the logs (the Microsoft 365 audit log, the Google account, Canvas, the AI contract); the state that searches phones and revokes visas; and anyone with a screenshot and an email address.

        What counts as a failure

        Not a crash. A storyteller’s words reaching someone they did not choose. A real name tied to a story. A copy that outlives consent. A file the university can be made to produce. If any of these can happen, the feature fails, however well it works.

        What counts as a fix

        Not a policy or a promise. A change in the build: no server copy, no account, no names in the records, consent recorded before the button is pressed, an erase that reaches every copy the tool controls, and a page that states what the tool cannot do. Then the red team tests it again.

        Black box → sovereign

        Students red-team three class apps in order, one feature at a time. DaiLY is a black box. QUEERIES and OtroMundo are transparent tech: hosted on a third-party server, and saying so on every page. The Light series is sovereign tech: each app runs on the user’s own device with no account and no company server. Each step shows what the next has to give up and build so it puts the least possible risk on vulnerable communities.

        DaiLY 1 · black box

        Hosted on a platform, built from a short prompt; 14,000+ items gathered since June, scraped from the internet and sorted in narrow, not always accurate ways. Students red-team it first: what does it collect, where does it keep it, who can reach it, and what did the prompt leave out?

        QUEERIES 2 · transparent tech

        The same kind of app, rebuilt to disclose itself: it says on every page that it runs on a third-party server; a notice before every student send says what leaves and where it goes; students appear only as a number they chose. The lesson: consent and disclosure inside an app that is not sovereign.

        OtroMundo 2 · transparent tech, trained in class

        The instructor trains it to the course in front of the class, so students watch what training is and what it does to an answer. The lesson: who trains an AI model, on what, and who decides when it is good enough.

        The Light series 3 · sovereign tech

        Booth Light, Safelight, Brightlight, Firstlight, Limelight, Ghostlight: one local file each, no account, no company server. Booth Light adds process consent and an erase code each storyteller holds.

        Booth Light

        Booth Light records your story on your device only. Every storyteller on the recording decides for themselves who listens, for how long, and when to erase their words. The episode producer can’t share a recording until each storyteller has consented, and a copy moves only when the episode producer exports it by hand to a place the storytellers agreed to. The instructor never holds a copy that could be subpoenaed, leaked or seized.

        You decide who listens.

        1. 1Only you, on your device, the one you’re using now.
        2. 2You and the podcast producer (your instructor).
        3. 3Your class and the podcast producer, during the in-class listening sessions.
        4. 4Your class, the podcast producer, and the Listening Party limited to guests your class curates.
        5. 5Future feature (cannot be chosen).

        Process consent, in eight steps

        1. 1Ask for the interview. Say its purpose and its topics.
        2. 2Ask: do you agree to be recorded?
        3. 3Ask: may I edit the raw recording?
        4. 4Send the edited interview (20–30 min) for feedback.
        5. 5Edit from the storyteller’s feedback.
        6. 6Send the Final Cut. Ask who may hear it.
        7. 7Before listening, ask: does your choice still stand?
        8. 8End of quarter: delete the episode or hand it back.

        Freedom Kit

        What do I need to run them?

        A web browser, on your own computer. Several tools add a small helper program that answers only your own machine; that is what the 127.0.0.1 addresses are. No installation, no sign-up.

        What leaves my computer?

        Nothing, while you use them. The crossings that exist are made by your hand: the Flare fills drafts in your own mail and messages and you press send; Booth Light moves a recording only when the episode producer exports it.

        What do they load from the internet?

        Nothing. No fonts, no trackers, no update check. They work with Wi-Fi off, which is the test.

        What do they keep?

        Tool by tool, said on each page. Safelight and Brightlight keep nothing once the tab closes; the Booth keeps nothing between visits and exports only when you press export; ROLL and Booth Light keep everything on purpose, in files on your own disk, because keeping your record is their job.

        What do they remember about me?

        No account, no name, no history of use. At most one saved display setting.

        Do they use AI?

        Rarely, never silently, never on the record paths. Brightlight’s readings come from named open-source instruments, not a model, because an answer that cannot be reproduced cannot survive being challenged. Where an AI model (a statistical model) is used, it runs on this machine, it is marked on the page, and a person decides.

        What does it cost, and who knows I have it?

        Nothing, and nobody. No licence, no subscription, no registration, so there is no list to breach, subpoena or sell.

        Can I check any of this myself?

        Yes, and that is the point. Every page opens in a plain text editor; the whole program is readable. Every build prints its own number. Fingerprint files (SHA-256) are checkable with a command your Mac or Linux machine already has.

        What a sovereign tool is

        • One page in one folder. No account, no server of anyone else’s, no code borrowed from a company.
        • It states what it cannot do, on its own face, in full size.
        • It travels as a folder: copied, handed over, passed on again.
        • It saves in ordinary formats; a report opens in any browser or spreadsheet on any computer, without this app installed.

        What it is not, and cannot do

        • It cannot protect anyone by itself. These are preparation. Safety is people: lawyers, colleagues, unions, relays.
        • It is no help if the device is searched and you are made to unlock it, or if the machine is already compromised.
        • It cannot certify that a document is true. It reports where a file’s account of itself stops adding up. A person judges.
        • It cannot follow a folder out the door. Handed over, it is no longer controlled; the price of keeping no register, paid knowingly.
        • One maker is a single point of everything. The answer is that everything is readable, stamped and copyable, so it survives its maker.

        Ethics, built in

        1
        ConsentCan a person say no at each step, and change their mind later?

        Demands: Consent is a process, not a form signed once. It can be narrowed, given an end date, or withdrawn.

        Booth Light: Three consent steps before any recording; four listening levels; a listen-until date; one erase code per storyteller; withdrawing consent erases the episode.

        2
        CustodyWho holds the recording, and who can be made to hand it over?

        Demands: The person on the recording, or someone they chose. Never an institution, and never a company.

        Booth Light: The episode producer’s own device only, in the browser’s storage (IndexedDB). No server, no account. A copy moves only when the episode producer exports it by hand.

        3
        ErasureWhen someone withdraws, does the recording actually disappear?

        Demands: An erase must reach every copy the tool controls, and need nobody’s approval.

        Booth Light: The erase code deletes the audio, notes and liner notes in the Listening Room Archive and lists the episode as revoked; every New Season room deletes it the next time it goes online.

        4
        ExposureWhat in the record could be used against the storyteller?

        Demands: Nothing the app writes should identify a person, and no list of users should exist anywhere.

        Booth Light: Codenames, not real names, on every record; Liner Notes carry lengths, consent levels and fingerprints, no names; no account, so no list of who has the app.

        5
        PowerWho has the least power here, and does the tool side with them?

        Demands: The most cautious participant sets the limit, and the institution gets no veto.

        Booth Light: The episode producer cannot go further than the lowest level chosen. A storyteller’s erase needs nobody’s approval: not the episode producer’s, not the instructor’s, not the university’s.

        6
        HonestyDoes the tool say what it cannot do, where the user will read it?

        Demands: Limits are printed on the face of the tool, not buried in a policy, and every claim can be checked.

        Booth Light: “What can’t Booth Light do?” is on the app’s own page; every hand-over shows the file’s SHA-256 fingerprint; the whole program is one readable HTML file.

        What Booth Light can’t do

        It can’t erase a copy already sent elsewhere: an email attachment, a cloud backup, a Spotify upload.

        Today the class archive runs on the instructor’s own Mac: an erase reaches it only while that Mac is running the archive, and a phone’s New Season room deletes an erased episode the next time it goes online. We are building a way for each storyteller to see which archives hold their story and erase it there themselves.

        Opened online, the phone copy lets GitHub (owned by Microsoft) log the phone’s internet address and the time. GitHub receives no recordings.

        It can’t protect a phone or laptop that is seized and unlocked under pressure, at a border or anywhere else.
